text: I'm 24 and I got a job offer abroad with double the salary, but my father is ill and my mother wants me to stay. Should I take the job or stay home?

Viveka's application - Recommendation: When duties conflict, name the confusion. Arjuna's duties to family, teachers and his role collide; he says plainly that his mind is confused about what is right and asks for one clear answer. The Gita begins from that honesty.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (you said you are 24; this involves your mother, father): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to conflicting duties.
  In practice: You are weighing 'take the job' against 'stay home'. Since this involves your mother, think about what they need as well as what you need. Ask which can be partly met, which can wait, and which cannot be compromised.

Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."
Source text (BG.3.2): "With words that seem mixed, you seem to confuse my mind. So tell me, decisively, the one thing by which I may reach what is best."
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Summarises 2.6-2.8: Arjuna reasons that being killed by the Kauravas would be better than an unrighteous victory; then, utterly helpless, he takes refuge at Krishna's feet and asks, as his disciple, to be told what is truly good for him.

  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Telling him to act, the opposite of the knowledge that withdraws the senses, seems contradictory, so Arjuna asks for one unmixed teaching he can follow.

  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to look for one authority to decide everything.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Your claim is to the work, not its results. Put your full effort into what is yours to do, and loosen your grip on how it turns out; outcomes depend on many factors you do not control.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (you said you are 22): addresses the kind of problem you describe; echoes your words: exam, result, wait.
  In practice: List what is in your control this week (preparation, effort, honesty) and what is not (the examiner, the market, other people). Judge yourself only on the first list.

Source text (BG.2.47): "Your right is to the work alone, never to its results. Do not let the results be your motive, and do not become attached to doing nothing."
Source text (BG.2.48): "Established in yoga, do your work, Arjuna, giving up attachment and staying the same in success and failure. This evenness of mind is called yoga."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Arjuna's entitlement is to action, not yet to the path of pure knowledge. Never thirst for results, because acting from that thirst makes one a cause of further birth; but this must not become a liking for inaction either.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Work done for its fruit binds; work done without desire for fruit, as worship of the Lord, leads to liberation. One should also reflect that one is not the sole doer: agency rests with the guṇas or with the Lord.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): The ban on acting for results applies even to the wise, and all the more to others, since results do not depend on oneself alone. Scripture's promises of rewards are only an inducement, like sweetening medicine.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Act only for the Lord's sake, giving up even the attachment 'may the Lord be pleased with me'. Success here is the purity of mind that leads to knowledge; staying even in success and failure is itself the yoga.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Give up attachment to kingdom and kin and do your work, such as fighting, even-minded about victory or defeat; yoga here is this evenness, a settled mind.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): Clarifies the previous verse: yoga is the means; giving up fondness for results makes one even in success and failure.

Historical example: Tilak reads the Gita as a call to action. Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote the Gita Rahasya (published 1915), reportedly while imprisoned in Mandalay, arguing that the Gita's central teaching is energetic, selfless action (karma yoga) rather than renunciation. Lesson: In a time of political struggle, a reader found in the Gita a mandate for engaged, selfless action in the world. Limits: Tilak's reading is one interpretation among several; it was shaped by his political context. (Not yet verified against its source.)

text: I was laid off at 45 after twenty years. I feel useless and I don't know who I am without my job.
rendered:
[DRAFT: internal test answer using unreviewed material. Not for users.]

Viveka's application - Recommendation: You are more than your body and roles. The self passes through childhood, youth and old age without being any of them; the body is the field, and you are its knower.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (we inferred the householder stage from 'my job'; tell us if that is wrong): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to meaning and direction; echoes your words: job, without; fits the householder stage (our inference).
  In practice: Write 'I am…' ten times, then cross out every answer that could be taken away. Notice what remains.

Source text (BG.13.1): "This body, son of Kunti, is called the field; the one who knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know these things."
Source text (BG.13.29): "One who sees that all actions are done entirely by nature, and that the self is not the doer, truly sees."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): The body is called the field because it is protected from harm, because it decays, or because the fruits of action grow in it like crops in a field.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): This chapter gathers up and distinguishes the knowledge, the knowable, the field and the person spoken of earlier.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Prakṛti is the Lord's three-guna māyā; it alone, transformed into body and senses, performs all actions of speech, mind and body.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): One who sees all actions as done by prakṛti (13.20), and the self as not the doer but of the nature of knowledge, sees rightly.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): And sees the self as not the doer.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita) on BG.13.1.

Historical example (story from the texts): What happens to one who tries and fails?. Arjuna asks what becomes of someone with faith who strives but falls short, fearing they perish 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin; they begin again from where they were. Lesson: Voicing the fear of failure invites a better answer than silent dread; effort carries forward. Limits: Krishna's answer speaks of future births; the modern application is narrower: skills and character built by effort remain even when a result fails.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: No sincere effort is wasted. Effort towards the good is never lost, even when it falls short; a person who tries and slips comes to no ruin and can start again from where they were.
  Source text (BG.2.40): "On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to neglect the body or dismiss real limitations.

text: My mother passed away last month and I can't stop crying. I'm 38 and I feel lost.
rendered:
[DRAFT: internal test answer using unreviewed material. Not for users.]

Viveka's application - Recommendation: The self is not destroyed when the body dies. The self is unborn and undying; as a person changes worn-out clothes, the embodied self passes from body to body. Weapons, fire, water and wind cannot touch it.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (you said you are 38; this involves your mother): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to grief and loss; echoes your words: lost, pass.
  In practice: If this teaching comforts you, let it sit beside your grief rather than replace it; keep talking about the person you lost.

Source text (BG.2.22): "As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws away worn-out bodies and enters new ones."
Source text (BG.2.23): "Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Like the person who changes clothes, the self remains unchanged as it leaves old bodies and takes on new ones.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Scripture teaches that those who give up the body in a righteous war gain a better one, so this is cause for joy, like exchanging worn clothes for fine new ones.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): An illustration to help one experience the self as distinct from the body.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Having no parts, the self cannot be divided by weapons, burned to ash, loosened by water or dried out by wind.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): The self pervades all the elements and is subtler than them, so they cannot pervade it; and cutting, burning, wetting and drying work only on what they pervade.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): Even something that does not perish of itself might seem destructible by some special cause; this verse rules out such causes for the self.

Historical example (story from the texts): Arjuna lays down his bow. On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. He tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks to be taught. Lesson: When duties collide, the paralysis and grief are real and are described in full; the turning point is admitting confusion and asking for help. Limits: Arjuna's dilemma is about fighting a war as a warrior. It is never an argument for violence, and most modern dilemmas have options he did not have, such as delay, mediation or leaving.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: When you are lost, say so and ask. Arjuna's turning point comes when he admits his mind is confused about what is right and asks for clear guidance; learning begins with that admission.
  Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to make death seem harmless, to justify violence, or near anyone at risk of self-harm. It also says nothing about how to live with the absence. Restricted for under-18s and anyone in distress.

Viveka's application - One next step: If this teaching comforts you, let it sit beside your grief rather than replace it; keep talking about the person you lost.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Withstand the surge of desire and anger. Whoever can withstand the force of desire and anger here, in this life, is disciplined and happy.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to self-control.

Source text (BG.5.23): "One who can withstand the surge of desire and anger here, before leaving the body, is disciplined; that person is happy."
Source text (BG.5.26): "For ascetics who are free of desire and anger, who have controlled their minds and know the self, the peace of Brahman is near on every side."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): The surge of desire and anger can arise at any moment while one lives, so one must never relax one's guard until death; one who can withstand it is disciplined and happy.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): One who, through the joy of experiencing the self, can hold back the surge of desire and anger while still practising is fit for that experience.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): Desire is easiest to master in a human body; higher worlds such as Brahmā's are reached only by those who have conquered desire.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): For renunciants free of desire and anger who know the self, liberation is present on both sides: while living and after death.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote the Gita Rahasya (published 1915), reportedly while imprisoned in Mandalay, arguing that the Gita's central teaching is energetic, selfless action (karma yoga) rather than renunciation.   Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Forgiveness is a mind unchanged towards others even when they cause one pain; fortitude is holding to what must be done even in great adversity.

After seeing Krishna's cosmic form, Arjuna asks forgiveness for every time he spoke carelessly to him as a mere friend, joking or disrespectful, alone or in front of others, asking him to bear with him as a father with a son, a friend with a friend. Lesson: Familiarity can make us careless with those closest to us; a specific, unguarded apology repairs it. Viveka's application - Recommendation: The self is not destroyed when the body dies. The self is unborn and undying; as a person changes worn-out clothes, the embodied self passes from body to body. Weapons, fire, water and wind cannot touch it.

  In practice: If this teaching comforts you, let it sit beside your grief rather than replace it; keep talking about the person you lost.

Source text (BG.2.22): "As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws away worn-out bodies and enters new ones."

Viveka's application - Recommendation: No sincere effort is wasted. Effort towards the good is never lost, even when it falls short; a person who tries and slips comes to no ruin and can start again from where they were.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (you said you are 30): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to a setback; echoes your words: fail.
  In practice: Write down three things your effort built that remain even though the result failed (skills, habits, relationships). Restart from those, not from zero.

Source text (BG.2.40): "On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear."
Source text (BG.6.40): "Son of Pritha, there is no destruction for such a person, neither in this world nor in the next; for no one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Karma yoga, even begun and broken off, is not fruitless and brings no penalty; even a small part protects from the fear of rebirth. He links this to 6.40.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Destruction here means a birth lower than before, which does not happen to one fallen from yoga. Krishna calls Arjuna 'tāta', a word for a son, since a father extends himself in his son.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): For one who began yoga with faith and fell away, there is no loss in either world: neither failure to gain what was desired nor meeting with harm.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.2.40; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.6.40.

Historical example (story from the texts): What happens to one who tries and fails?. Arjuna asks what becomes of someone with faith who strives but falls short, fearing they perish 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin; they begin again from where they were. Lesson: Voicing the fear of failure invites a better answer than silent dread; effort carries forward. Limits: Krishna's answer speaks of future births; the modern application is narrower: skills and character built by effort remain even when a result fails.

text: I'm 35 with two small kids and I want to leave everything and live in an ashram. Is that the spiritual thing to do?
rendered:
[DRAFT: internal test answer using unreviewed material. Not for users.]

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Renounce selfish intent, not your responsibilities. A true renunciant is one who does what should be done without depending on its fruit, who neither hates nor craves; what they call renunciation is giving up selfish intentions.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (we inferred the householder stage from 'with two small kids'; tell us if that is wrong; you said you are 35; this involves your kids): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to meaning and direction; echoes your words: spiritual; fits the householder stage (our inference).
  In practice: Since this involves your kids, think about what they need as well as what you need. Keep your commitments, and look for the selfish intention inside them that you could let go of instead.

Source text (BG.6.1): "One who does the work that should be done, without depending on its fruit, is a renunciant and a yogi; not one who merely gives up the sacred fire, nor one who gives up action."
Source text (BG.6.2): "What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, son of Pandu; for no one becomes a yogi without renouncing selfish intentions."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): One who does their regular duty without thirst for its fruit is both renunciant and yogi; not merely someone who has given up the sacred fires and rites.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): One who acts, not for rewards like heaven, but because worshipping the Supreme Person, our friend, is itself the goal, is both a renunciant (devoted to knowledge) and a yogi (devoted to action).
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): This chapter teaches the yoga of meditation, close to knowledge. Even monks have their 'fire' and rites: Brahman and its worship.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): The true renunciation known to scripture, giving up all actions and their fruits, is likened to the yoga of action because no one becomes a yogi without giving up intentions.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): What they call the path of knowledge, know to be karma yoga itself: through reflecting on the true self, one gives up the intention of taking prakṛti to be the self.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): Renunciation is contained within yoga: without giving up desire and intention, how could anyone have the means?

Historical example (story from the texts): Janaka reached perfection through action. Krishna cites King Janaka and others who reached perfection while acting in the world, and urges Arjuna to act with an eye to holding the world together. text: We lost our biggest client and my small business might fail. I feel like a failure as a provider.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: No sincere effort is wasted. Effort towards the good is never lost, even when it falls short; a person who tries and slips comes to no ruin and can start again from where they were.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to a setback; echoes your words: fail, lost.
  In practice: Write down three things your effort built that remain even though the result failed (skills, habits, relationships). Restart from those, not from zero.

Source text (BG.2.40): "On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear."
Source text (BG.6.40): "Son of Pritha, there is no destruction for such a person, neither in this world nor in the next; for no one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Karma yoga, even begun and broken off, is not fruitless and brings no penalty; even a small part protects from the fear of rebirth. He links this to 6.40.

  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): For one who began yoga with faith and fell away, there is no loss in either world: neither failure to gain what was desired nor meeting with harm.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.2.40; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.6.40.

Historical example (story from the texts): What happens to one who tries and fails?. Arjuna asks what becomes of someone with faith who strives but falls short, fearing they perish 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin; they begin again from where they were. Lesson: Voicing the fear of failure invites a better answer than silent dread; effort carries forward. Limits: Krishna's answer speaks of future births; the modern application is narrower: skills and character built by effort remain even when a result fails.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: Ask your fear of failure out loud. Arjuna asks what becomes of one who tries and fails, 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin.

text: My wife wants us to move to her hometown, but my career is here. I can't decide.
rendered:
[DRAFT: internal test answer using unreviewed material. Not for users.]

Viveka's application - Recommendation: When duties conflict, name the confusion. Arjuna's duties to family, teachers and his role collide; he says plainly that his mind is confused about what is right and asks for one clear answer. The Gita begins from that honesty.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (we inferred the householder stage from 'my wife'; tell us if that is wrong; this involves your wife): addresses the kind of problem you describe; echoes your words: career; fits the householder stage (our inference).
  In practice: Since this involves your wife, think about what they need as well as what you need. Write each duty and to whom it is owed. Ask which can be partly met, which can wait, and which cannot be compromised.

Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."
Source text (BG.3.2): "With words that seem mixed, you seem to confuse my mind. So tell me, decisively, the one thing by which I may reach what is best."
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Summarises 2.6-2.8: Arjuna reasons that being killed by the Kauravas would be better than an unrighteous victory; then, utterly helpless, he takes refuge at Krishna's feet and asks, as his disciple, to be told what is truly good for him.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Krishna speaks clearly, but to Arjuna's limited understanding the words seem mixed: the one who came to remove his confusion seems to add to it.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Telling him to act, the opposite of the knowledge that withdraws the senses, seems contradictory, so Arjuna asks for one unmixed teaching he can follow.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Śaṅkara (Advaita) on BG.2.7; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.2.7; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.3.2.

Historical example (story from the texts): Arjuna lays down his bow. On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. He tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks to be taught. Lesson: When duties collide, the paralysis and grief are real and are described in full; the turning point is admitting confusion and asking for help. Limits: Arjuna's dilemma is about fighting a war as a warrior. It is never an argument for violence, and most modern dilemmas have options he did not have, such as delay, mediation or leaving.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: Reflect fully, then choose for yourself. After teaching everything, Krishna tells Arjuna: 'Reflect on it fully, then do as you choose.' The final decision is the person's own.
  Source text (BG.18.63): "Thus I have taught you wisdom more secret than all secrets. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you choose."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to look for one authority to decide everything.

Viveka's application - One next step: Write each duty and to whom it is owed. Ask which can be partly met, which can wait, and which cannot be compromised.

  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.

  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to conflicting duties; echoes your words: part.

Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."
Source text (BG.3.2): "With words that seem mixed, you seem to confuse my mind. So tell me, decisively, the one thing by which I may reach what is best."
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Summarises 2.6-2.8: Arjuna reasons that being killed by the Kauravas would be better than an unrighteous victory; then, utterly helpless, he takes refuge at Krishna's feet and asks, as his disciple, to be told what is truly good for him.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Krishna speaks clearly, but to Arjuna's limited understanding the words seem mixed: the one who came to remove his confusion seems to add to it.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Telling him to act, the opposite of the knowledge that withdraws the senses, seems contradictory, so Arjuna asks for one unmixed teaching he can follow.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Śaṅkara (Advaita) on BG.2.7; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.2.7; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.3.2.

On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. He tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks to be taught. Lesson: When duties collide, the paralysis and grief are real and are described in full; the turning point is admitting confusion and asking for help. Limits: Arjuna's dilemma is about fighting a war as a warrior. It is never an argument for violence, and most modern dilemmas have options he did not have, such as delay, mediation or leaving.

  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): However devotees conceive of me and take refuge, I show myself to them in that way; all people long to follow me, and I let even their ordinary eyes see my nature.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Nourish one another. 'Nourishing one another, you will reach the highest good': mutual care is the basic pattern of a good life.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe.

Source text (BG.3.11): "With this, nourish the gods, and let the gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you will reach the highest good."
Source text (BG.10.9): "With minds fixed on me and lives given to me, enlightening one another and always speaking of me, they are content and full of joy."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Nourish Indra and the other gods with sacrifice, and they will nourish you with rain; so you will reach the highest good, liberation through knowledge, or else heaven.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): The gods are Krishna's body and have him as their self; worshipped through sacrifice, they sustain you, and so you reach liberation. He cites 9.24.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Their minds are on me and their senses drawn into me, or their very life is me; they teach one another and speak of me, finding contentment and delight.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Unable to live without me, they tell one another of the qualities of mine they have experienced and of my lovely deeds, and find contentment and joy.

Historical example (story from the texts): Arjuna lays down his bow. On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. He tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right and asks to be taught. Lesson: When duties collide, the paralysis and grief are real and are described in full; the turning point is admitting confusion and asking for help. Limits: Arjuna's dilemma is about fighting a war as a warrior. It is never an argument for violence, and most modern dilemmas have options he did not have, such as delay, mediation or leaving.

  Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It obliges someone to keep nourishing a relationship that only harms them.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Fearlessness is the first of the divine qualities. Fearlessness heads the list of divine qualities; Krishna tells the frightened Arjuna not to be afraid, and the yogi sits calm and fearless.
  Why it fits you: For your situation (we inferred the householder stage from 'my husband'; tell us if that is wrong; this involves your husband): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to fear and anxiety; echoes your words: afraid; fits the householder stage (our inference).
  In practice: Your safety comes first. Quietly prepare: keep your ID, important papers, some money and a charged phone where you can reach them; tell one trusted person what is happening; and save a help-line number. Leaving can be planned step by step, and the help lines can advise on shelter and money, so dependence does not have to trap you. Take one small brave action today that you have been avoiding out of fear.

Source text (BG.16.1): "Fearlessness, purity of heart, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, generosity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of scripture, austerity, honesty,"
Source text (BG.6.14): "calm and fearless, firm in the vow of celibacy, controlling the mind and thinking of me, one should sit disciplined, intent on me."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Fearlessness is freedom from fear; purity of heart means dealing with others without deceit, trickery or falsehood; steadfastness in knowledge is firm, focused understanding of the self gained from scripture and teacher.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Fear is the distress that comes from seeing a cause of losing the wanted or meeting the unwanted; fearlessness is its absence. Generosity is giving rightly earned wealth to a worthy recipient.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): This chapter shows what opposes the means to life's goals; 'austerity' here means celibacy and the like.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Fearless, keeping the student's vow (celibacy, serving the teacher, living on alms), with the mind withdrawn and fixed on me, the Supreme Lord.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita) on BG.6.14; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.6.14.

Historical example (story from the texts): Arjuna's doubts resolve. After the whole dialogue, Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect fully and choose for himself. Arjuna says his delusion is gone, he stands firm, and he will act. Lesson: Good counsel ends by returning the decision to the person; clarity is meant to end in action. Limits: Arjuna's action is going to war; the parallel is only in the structure of deciding after reflection.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: Reflect fully, then choose for yourself. After teaching everything, Krishna tells Arjuna: 'Reflect on it fully, then do as you choose.' The final decision is the person's own.
  Source text (BG.18.63): "Thus I have taught you wisdom more secret than all secrets. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you choose."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is confused with recklessness, or used to shame someone for normal fear.

Viveka's application - One next step: Today, save one help-line number where it is safe to keep it, and tell one person you trust what is happening.

text: All my friends got rich on crypto. I'm thinking of putting all my savings in. Should I?
questions: What are the main options you are choosing between?
rendered:
[DRAFT: internal test answer using unreviewed material. Not for users.]

Questions that could change this answer:
  - What are the main options you are choosing between?

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Weigh consequences, harm and your own capacity. Action begun without regard for its consequences, the loss it causes, harm to others or one's own capacity comes from delusion.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to conflicting duties; echoes your words: think.
  In practice: Because money or dependency is involved, check what you can afford and secure that before any big move. Before acting, write four lines: likely consequences, what it could cost, who could be hurt, and whether you can actually carry it through.

Source text (BG.18.25): "Action undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one's own capacity, is called tamasic."
Source text (BG.18.30): "The understanding that knows when to act and when to refrain, what should and should not be done, what is to be feared and what is not, and what binds and what frees, son of Pritha, is sattvic."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Action begun without regard to its consequences, to the loss of strength or wealth it causes, to harm to living beings, or to whether one can finish it, is tamasic.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Action begun without weighing the suffering that follows, the loss of wealth, harm to beings, or one's ability to finish it, out of not knowing that the Supreme Person is the doer, is tamasic.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Engagement is the path of action, which binds; withdrawal is the path of renunciation, which frees; sattvic understanding knows these, what to do and avoid, and what to fear and not.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Engagement is dharma that brings prosperity; withdrawal is dharma that brings liberation; sattvic understanding knows both and what is to be done in each place, time and situation.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.18.25; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.18.30.

Historical example: Tilak reads the Gita as a call to action. Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote the Gita Rahasya (published 1915), reportedly while imprisoned in Mandalay, arguing that the Gita's central teaching is energetic, selfless action (karma yoga) rather than renunciation. Lesson: In a time of political struggle, a reader found in the Gita a mandate for engaged, selfless action in the world. Limits: Tilak's reading is one interpretation among several; it was shaped by his political context. (Not yet verified against its source.)

Offered three boons by Death, Nachiketas uses the first to ask that his angry father be calm, free of anger towards him, and welcome him home. Death grants it.   Why it fits you: For your situation (you said you are 17; this involves your parents): addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to a setback; echoes your words: fail.

Source text (BG.2.40): "On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear."
Source text (BG.6.40): "Son of Pritha, there is no destruction for such a person, neither in this world nor in the next; for no one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: Weigh consequences, harm and your own capacity. Action begun without regard for its consequences, the loss it causes, harm to others or one's own capacity comes from delusion.

Source text (BG.18.25): "Action undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one's own capacity, is called tamasic."

  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Action begun without regard to its consequences, to the loss of strength or wealth it causes, to harm to living beings, or to whether one can finish it, is tamasic.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Action begun without weighing the suffering that follows, the loss of wealth, harm to beings, or one's ability to finish it, out of not knowing that the Supreme Person is the doer, is tamasic.

Quietly prepare: keep your ID, important papers, some money and a charged phone where you can reach them; tell one trusted person what is happening; and save a help-line number.   Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Reads 'self' here as the mind: a mind not attached to sense objects lifts a person up, while an attached mind drags them down. The mind alone is friend or enemy.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: When duties conflict, name the confusion. Arjuna's duties to family, teachers and his role collide; he says plainly that his mind is confused about what is right and asks for one clear answer. The Gita begins from that honesty.

Source text (BG.2.7): "My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me."

On the eve of battle, Arjuna sees teachers and relatives on the other side, is overcome with grief and pity, trembles, drops his bow and refuses to act. Source text (IsU.7): "When, for one who knows, all beings have become the Self, what delusion, what grief can there be for one who sees oneness?"
Source text (KaU.2.1.5): "Whoever knows this Self, the one who tastes the honey, the living one, close at hand, lord of past and future, no longer seeks to shield himself. This, truly, is that."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Grief and delusion, the seeds of desire and action, belong to one who does not know. For one who sees the oneness of the Self, pure like the sky, they cannot arise, and so worldly existence is uprooted together with its cause.

Death offers Nachiketas long-lived descendants, wealth, kingship, long life and every pleasure if he will drop his question about what lies beyond death. Nachiketas replies that these fade, that no one is satisfied by wealth, and that he wants only the answer. Lesson: Holding on to what truly matters, even when offered attractive substitutes. Limits: Not every attractive offer is a temptation away from the good; sometimes the comfortable option is also the right one.

If your coach has a say over your home, money or safety, plan for how they may react and who could support you. Source text (BG.18.25): "Action undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one's own capacity, is called tamasic."
Source text (BG.18.30): "The understanding that knows when to act and when to refrain, what should and should not be done, what is to be feared and what is not, and what binds and what frees, son of Pritha, is sattvic."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Action begun without regard to its consequences, to the loss of strength or wealth it causes, to harm to living beings, or to whether one can finish it, is tamasic.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Action begun without weighing the suffering that follows, the loss of wealth, harm to beings, or one's ability to finish it, out of not knowing that the Supreme Person is the doer, is tamasic.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Engagement is the path of action, which binds; withdrawal is the path of renunciation, which frees; sattvic understanding knows these, what to do and avoid, and what to fear and not.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Engagement is dharma that brings prosperity; withdrawal is dharma that brings liberation; sattvic understanding knows both and what is to be done in each place, time and situation.

Historical example: Tilak reads the Gita as a call to action. Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote the Gita Rahasya (published 1915), reportedly while imprisoned in Mandalay, arguing that the Gita's central teaching is energetic, selfless action (karma yoga) rather than renunciation. Lesson: In a time of political struggle, a reader found in the Gita a mandate for engaged, selfless action in the world. Limits: Tilak's reading is one interpretation among several; it was shaped by his political context. (Not yet verified against its source.)

text: Is it wrong to want more money?

Viveka's application - Recommendation: No one is satisfied by wealth. Desire is as hard to satisfy as fire; Nachiketas observes that no one is ever satisfied by wealth.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe; speaks to money or success; echoes your words: money.
  In practice: Because money or dependency is involved, check what you can afford and secure that before any big move. Write down the amount that would be 'enough' and what you would do differently once you have it. Ask whether you could start some of it now.

Source text (KaU.1.1.27): "No one is satisfied by wealth. We shall have wealth if we have seen you; we shall live as long as you rule. But the boon I would choose is that one alone."
Source text (BG.3.39): "Wisdom is covered by this constant enemy of the wise, son of Kunti: by desire, which is as hard to satisfy as fire."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): No one in the world is ever seen to be satisfied by gaining wealth. Having met Death, wealth and life will come anyway; the only boon worth choosing is knowledge of the Self.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Desire is the constant enemy of the wise in particular: the wise know beforehand that it leads to harm, while the fool sees it as a friend until the suffering comes.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Desire covers the self's knowledge by producing infatuation with objects, and it can never be satisfied.
  Commentator's view - Madhva (Dvaita): Even knowledge gained from scripture fails to reveal the Supreme directly when covered by desire; desire is hard to fill and never says 'enough'.
  Commentator's view - No commentary by Madhva (Dvaita) or Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita) on the Katha Upanishad is in the library yet.

Historical example (story from the texts): Nachiketas turns down every temptation. Death offers Nachiketas long-lived descendants, wealth, kingship, long life and every pleasure if he will drop his question about what lies beyond death. Nachiketas replies that these fade, that no one is satisfied by wealth, and that he wants only the answer. Lesson: Holding on to what truly matters, even when offered attractive substitutes. Limits: Not every attractive offer is a temptation away from the good; sometimes the comfortable option is also the right one.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: Give it, enjoy it, or lose it. Wealth has three courses: giving, enjoyment and loss; whoever neither gives nor enjoys it meets the third.
  Source text (NS.43): "Giving, enjoyment and loss: these are the three courses that wealth takes. Whoever neither gives nor enjoys it, theirs takes the third course."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to dismiss real poverty or the legitimate need for financial security.

Viveka's application - One next step: Write down the amount that would be 'enough' and what you would do differently once you have it. Ask whether you could start some of it now.

Viveka's application - Recommendation: No sincere effort is wasted. Effort towards the good is never lost, even when it falls short; a person who tries and slips comes to no ruin and can start again from where they were.
  Why it fits you: For your situation: addresses the kind of problem you describe.
  In practice: Write down three things your effort built that remain even though the result failed (skills, habits, relationships). Restart from those, not from zero.

Source text (BG.2.40): "On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear."
Source text (BG.6.40): "Son of Pritha, there is no destruction for such a person, neither in this world nor in the next; for no one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end."
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): Karma yoga, even begun and broken off, is not fruitless and brings no penalty; even a small part protects from the fear of rebirth. He links this to 6.40.
  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): Destruction here means a birth lower than before, which does not happen to one fallen from yoga. Krishna calls Arjuna 'tāta', a word for a son, since a father extends himself in his son.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): For one who began yoga with faith and fell away, there is no loss in either world: neither failure to gain what was desired nor meeting with harm.
  Commentator's view - Our source has no comment from Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.2.40; Madhva (Dvaita) on BG.6.40.

Historical example (story from the texts): What happens to one who tries and fails?. Arjuna asks what becomes of someone with faith who strives but falls short, fearing they perish 'like a scattered cloud'. Krishna answers that no one who does good comes to ruin; they begin again from where they were. Lesson: Voicing the fear of failure invites a better answer than silent dread; effort carries forward. Limits: Krishna's answer speaks of future births; the modern application is narrower: skills and character built by effort remain even when a result fails.

Viveka's application - Strongest alternative: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: A cut tree grows again. A tree that is cut grows again, and the waning moon fills again; reflecting on this, the good are not crushed by misfortune.
  Source text (NS.87): "A tree, though cut, grows again; the moon, though waning, fills again. Reflecting on this, the good are not tormented by misfortune."
  When the recommended principle misleads: It is used to keep pouring effort into a path that is clearly wrong for the person (sunk cost).

  Commentator's view - Śaṅkara (Advaita): One who does their regular duty without thirst for its fruit is both renunciant and yogi; not merely someone who has given up the sacred fires and rites.
  Commentator's view - Rāmānuja (Viśiṣṭādvaita): One who acts, not for rewards like heaven, but because worshipping the Supreme Person, our friend, is itself the goal, is both a renunciant (devoted to knowledge) and a yogi (devoted to action).
